topics.title: Made up Math Problem
topics.text:
Albert recently bought a book called "The House of Silk." After he read part of the book, he decided that he did enough reading for the day and wanted to play some video games, so he got out his phone, walked outside, and started playing pokemon-go. Later, when he was finished playing pokemon-go, he went back to his house and decided that he wanted to read some more before going to sleep, only to realize that he didn't save the page he was on when he closed the book. He knows these clues:



1. The page he was on is a 3-digit number.



2. There are 296 pages total



3. All  the digits of the page number he was on is either prime or composite



4. The digits are in ascending order from left to right.



But, it turns out that Albert has bad memory and knows that exactly one of these clues are wrong. How many possibilities are there for the page number Albert was on?

topics.title: Amazing Algebra!
topics.text:
Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ satisfy these equations:

$$\alpha=\alpha^2-\beta^2$$and $$\beta=\alpha^2+\beta^2$$Find all possible ordered pairs $(\alpha, \beta)$.

A bit of start finding alpha$\alpha+\beta=2\alpha^2$. So, $\alpha=(2\alpha^2)(\alpha-\beta)$. Subtracting gives $\alpha-\beta=-2\beta^2$, so $\alpha=-4\alpha^2\beta^2$.

topics.title: moab33's Math Tips #3: Alternate Polygons
topics.text:
So, when I was taking Geometry in Prealgebra, I was like, "I don't understand how this triangle dissection thing works!"

So, a few months ago, using that result that the sum of angles in a polygon is $180(n-2)$, I came up with this simpler idea:

"I want to find the angle of a regular $k$-sided polygon. I know that the sum of angles is $180(k-2)$. So I'll divide by $k$, giving $180-\frac{360}{k}$. Aha! This makes sense!"

Think why is makes sense. It's kind of programming, but if we have a robotic point, instead of going straight, it says "Turn $\frac{360}{k}$ degrees". But of course it's turning $\frac{360}{k}$ degrees! Repeat that $k$ times and it's clear that you have the polygon!

This is why I like to use this way: it's much clearer. And, we can get back to the original sum of angles by reversing the processes.

And so, we can do a few things:

The angle in an equilateral triangle is $180-\frac{360}{3}=60$. That was easier than the first way!

The angle in a square is $180-\frac{360}{4}=90$.

The angle in a regular pentagon is $180-\frac{360}{5}=108$.

.

.

.

The angle in a regular $360$ sided shape is $180-1=179$. That was much easier than taking $180(360-2)$ and dividing by $360$ and going through the same process but with more steps.

Thank you for reading this math tip!



~moab33

topics.title: MATHCOUNTS Experience - 500th post
topics.text:
Hello, AoPS!

Very similar to fatant, I have utilized my 500th post to commemorate my MATHCOUNTS experience. I hope you enjoy, and good luck in all your endeavours! (Hope you like the title, lol)





The Final Countdown

Drumming my fingers in dull anticipation, I waited for the MATHCOUNTS Chapter Individual Awards Ceremony to finish. I was extremely anxious to find out whether or not my school team had qualified for the state competition. I knew I had little to no chance of placing, or qualifying for states, as an individual since I lived in Northern Virginia, filled with many of the country’s brightest minds.

Suddenly, I heard my name being called, albeit horribly butchered. In a daze, I collected an award without even knowing what I had just been recognized for. It was only when my teammate smiled and gave my two thumbs up that I realized I had just earned fifth place in one of the most competitive MATHCOUNTS chapters nationwide. It dimly registered in my mind that I had just qualified for the Virginia state competition off of my very own merit. I had finally accomplished my goal to make the Virginia State MATHCOUNTS Competition, and I traveled back to the moment when I first dreamt of this prospect.

My mom had taken me, then an enthusiastic fifth-grader, to the regional MATHCOUNTS competition to watch the sixteen top “Mathletes” participate in a lightning round, as well as the subsequent awards ceremony. My heart was full to the burst with excitement, and I had sat in anticipation for the “Countdown” Round, as it was called, to begin.

At first, the problems seemed relatively easy, and I mentally screamed at the competitors to go faster. However, when the 38th problem flashed on the screen, I was somewhat stumped. How was anyone supposed to solve this in 40 seconds?

                  What is the largest six-digit number with an odd number of positive factors?

I immediately knew that it had to be a perfect square. Within four seconds, though, one of the competitors buzzed in, and gave the correct answer, 998,001. A collective “Wow!” diffused through the room, and that was when it dawned upon me. I wanted to be smart like them one day, and be admired for my ingenuity.

Watching the awards ceremony further kindled my passion. I realized just how prestigious it was to make the state competition, and moreover, how unique and refreshing of an experience it would be. From that day onwards, I began furiously practicing math problems, with my goal of making the state competition in mind.

It was certainly not an easy feat to accomplish. First, I had to participate in 10 grueling qualification rounds just to make the 10-person school team. Then, I had to compete in the chapter competition amongst 225 intelligent students, and place somewhere in top 10 students to even have the slightest chance of making the state competition.

In sixth grade, 2015, thanks to all of my practice, I edged out as 1st place, team captain, in my elementary school’s team. However, at the chapter competition, since there were so many middle schools with extremely talented students, I didn’t stand a chance. Although I was disappointed, I continued to practice. Daily, I hung out with my favorites, algebra and number theory, while tackling my weaknesses, geometry and counting & probability.

The next year, 2016, I qualified to my middle school’s team in 5th place. I found the problems significantly easier and improved my score from the previous year by almost ten points. However, even this was not enough to advance to the state competition. After all, six people in the chapter had achieved perfect scores, whereas I was six points away from this. I came home pleased that I had improved my score, and ambitious to make states in my last year of eligibility.

This year, in eighth grade, it was particularly hard to prepare. Last year, we were easing into middle school life. Suddenly, we were being prepared to graduate from it, and we had enormous boatloads of homework and projects as a result. This was also the year that the debilitating TJHSST admissions process took place, which absorbed plenty of the time out of my schedule. To top it all, I was taking one of my core subjects, math, specifically Algebra II Honors, as an online course, and had to spend extra time to meet all of the course requirements.

Amidst all of this, I had to qualify for the school MATHCOUNTS team, worry about whether or not I made it in, and practice to make the state competition. When I found the time to practice problems, I did so, and utilized my winter break to brush up on my speed and accuracy.

Ah, February 4th, 2017. The day of my last-ever chapter competition, and possibly last-ever MATHCOUNTS competition, was stealthily approaching – or, in Latin, furtim appropinquabat. I solely concentrated on doing well enough to help my team advance to the state competition. I knew that with the competition from my own school and from other schools, my chances of ranking individually, however much I practiced, would be slim.

The first round, the Sprint Round, consisted of 30 word problems to be done in 40 minutes. I finished all 30 problems with little difficulty, although I had a slight doubt on the last two. Unfazed, I continued on to ace the Target Round. After completing the Team Round, I indulged myself in homemade quesadillas, pleased with my performance.

When lunch was finished, people were called for tiebreakers. Typically, if one is called for tiebreakers, this means that they have placed in the top 10 and need their ranks to be distinguished from their competitors’. My heart sank as I learned that I hadn’t been called for the tiebreakers, yet two of my teammates had been. Oh well, I thought, we’ll probably qualify as a team anyway.

Then, the anticipated results for the top 16 qualifying individuals to the Countdown Round were read out. As the list droned on, my name failed to appear. However, after the 14th person had been called, I heard my name. I went up to the front of the hall with an enormous, goofy grin on my face.

As I watched my fellow competitors race against each other and the clock, I chastised them for not being faster. Come on guys, the answer is 144, I would scream in my head.

Finally, my turn came. Unfortunately, as I later learned, I was paired against our chapter’s champion, who turned out to be a mental math genius. While I read two words of each problem, he had the answer. In defeat, I smiled and walked back to my seat. At least I had fulfilled half of my dream.

When the countdown round concluded, the awards commenced. It was then that I found out that my team members had actually been called for a tiebreaker within ranks 8, 9, and 10, and I had really gotten fifth place. Quite ironically, my school team, which I was expecting to earn second place and advance to states, came out in a disappointing fifth place. I qualified for states and was the only person in my school to do so. I have been practicing for the state competition, which is on March 18th, since then, in hopes of possibly making the Countdown Round there.

I learned so much throughout my MATHCOUNTS career. First, I realized that hard work and dedication, combined with passion, can help you achieve almost anything in life. I also now value the importance of perseverance. Finally, through firsthand experience, I learned that it is quite possible to hold a number of idiotic countenances as one walks up to receive recognition.

topics.title: Books, probability, and more book!
topics.text:
1) I am pulling $2$ books out of a pile of two genres. I have $50$ science fiction books and $50$ historical fiction books. What is the probability that I pull two of the same genre? (Genres cannot overlap.)

2) Now I'm pulling $3$ books out of a pile of two genres. I have $50$ science fiction books and $50$ historical fiction books. What is the probability that I pull three of the same genre? (Genres cannot overlap)

3) Uh oh. Now I have $3$ genres: $50$ of the books are historical fiction, $50$ books are science fiction, and the other $50$ are neither genre. I'm still pulling two books. What is the probability that I the books I pull are both of the same genre? (Genres can STILL not overlap.)

topics.title: A problem about cars and combonatorics
topics.text: Henry owns $20$ cars with $4$ colors: gray, blue, yellow and red, such that there are $5$ red cars, $5$ blue cars, $5$ yellow cars, and $5$ gray cars. He decides to arrange them in a circle such that if Car A is next to Car B, the cars cannot be the same color. He then numbers the cars such that all cars in the range Car $1$ to Car $5$ are gray, Car $6$ to Car $10$ is the red group, $11$ to $15$ is the yellow group, and $16$ to $20$ is blue. Then, he adds the condition that Car $n$ cannot be adjacent to Car $(2n\mod20)$. How many ways can Henry arrange his cars?

topics.title: 1995-96 Mathcounts National Team #4
topics.text:
How many ways are there to write seven-element data lists of integers in numerical order to fit the following criteria: the mean is $20$; the median is $21$; the mode is $22$ and unique; and the range is $10$?



What I didSince $22$ is a mode, there must be more than one $22$. There is also no space between the median, $21$ and $22$ because then $22$ wouldn't be unique. So the set order from least to greatest is...



$a \quad x \quad y \quad 21 \quad 22 \quad 22 \quad b$



I put $a$ and $b$ has the first and last variables because we are going to manipulate those since we have the range, which is $10$. The sum of the numbers is $20 \cdot 7 = 140$, so $a + x+y+21+22+22+b = 140 \Rightarrow a+x+y+b = 75$



Case 1:We start with the case that $a=12$ and $b=22$



$12 \quad x \quad y \quad 21 \quad 22 \quad 22 \quad 22$



This means that $x+y=41$ So $x=20$ and $y=21$ Its okay to have $21$ twice because there are $3$ $22$'s, making it unique. So we have 1 case



Case 2: Now we will do the case with $a=13$ and $b=23$



$13 \quad x \quad y \quad 21 \quad 22 \quad 22 \quad 23$



$x+y=39$. So the possible cases are $x=19$ and $y=20$. We can't have $y=21$ because the mode won't be unique. So we have 1 case



Case 3: $a=14$ $b=24$



$14 \quad x \quad y \quad 21 \quad 22 \quad 22 \quad 24$



$x+y=37$. The cases are $x=18$ and $y=19$ and $x=17$ and $y=20$. So there are 2 cases.



Case 4: $a=15$ $b=25$



$15 \quad x \quad y \quad 21 \quad 22 \quad 22 \quad 25$



$x+y=35$. We have cases $x=17$, $y=18$ and $x=16$, $y=19$. We can't have $x=15$, $y=20$ because then we will have $2$ $15$'s. So we have 2 cases.



Anything above that won't work, so we have $1+1+2+2 = \boxed{6}$ cases.




Answer$7$

topics.title: Probablity Problem with squares
topics.text:
I was watching 2 people play a countdown and the following problem came across the screen saying: Two positive integers less than 100 are selected at random what is the probability that they are both perfect squares. Well this is My thinkingIf you have to choose an integer that is positive and less than 100 then there are 99 possibilities  and there are also 9 perfect squares in the range of 1-99, so  wouldn't the answer be 9/99 which simplifies to be 1/11. That's my thinking.
, however my thinking is wrong and after a bit of digging around aops this was the solution that I managed to find: [There are 99 positive integers less than 100. Because the square root of 100 is 10, there are 9 perfect squares in this range. The desired probability is therefore the probability of choosing 2 of these 9 when choosing 2 from the 99, $\frac{\binom{9}{2}}{\binom{99}{2}}=\boxed{\frac{4}{539}}$\/b]

Please help me solve this.







Thanks,

ItzVineeth
